title: Signature Solution - Refining & Finishing
summary: Students judge their signature solution against accuracy, usefulness and risk, then make one improvement and prove with re-testing that it helped.
objectives: Finish the solution so it meets the agreed success criteria.
Evaluate it for accuracy, usefulness and risk.
Explain one change that improved it.

sections.heading: Overview
body: You are almost there. This week you become the judge of your own work, checking it for accuracy, usefulness and risk, then making one smart change that you can prove made it better.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can finish my solution so it meets the success criteria our class agreed on.
I can judge my solution for accuracy, usefulness and risk using the rubric.
I can explain one change I made and say why it made the solution better.

terms.definition: To improve something on purpose by comparing it to your goals.
How often the system gives the right or sensible answer.
How much the solution really helps the user do their task.
What could go wrong or who could be harmed, including privacy.
Proof from testing, not just an opinion.

sections.heading: Judging your solution three ways
body: A good builder does not just ask 'do I like it?'. You measure your work against the criteria the class agreed.
**Accuracy**: test with examples where you know the right answer. **Usefulness**: check it helps your real user. **Risk**: ask what could go wrong and whether any private data is exposed.

sections.label: Criteria card
sections.heading: The three lenses
sections.intro: Judge your solution through each lens in turn. A solution can be accurate and still fail the other two.

entries.asks: How often does it give the right or sensible answer?
entries.test: Test it with examples where you already know the correct answer, and record the score.

entries.asks: Does it actually help your user do their task?
entries.test: Check it against the real task you designed it for, not a task that happens to suit it.

entries.asks: What could go wrong, and who could be harmed?
entries.test: Check for unfair results and for any private data being exposed.

sections.heading: One change, proven
body: You do not need many changes. Choose the one improvement that matters most to your user.
Make the change, then re-test. If accuracy went up and nothing else broke, you have evidence it worked. Write it in your refinement note.

sections.label: How to prove a change worked
sections.heading: One change at a time, with evidence
sections.altText: A loop: judge the solution against the criteria, change one thing, run it again, and judge again to see whether that change helped.
sections.repeatLabel: still short of the criteria — go round again
sections.caption: Same input each time, one change each time. **Change two things at once and you cannot say which one worked** — which is the evidence you are being asked for.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Work with your partner. Judge your solution against the rubric, choose one improvement, make it, and prove it helped.
items: Read the three lenses on the criteria card.
Run one accuracy test with known answers and record the score.
Check usefulness against your real user's task.
Do a basic risk check for harm, fairness and privacy.
Pick one improvement, make it, and re-test.
Swap for 'two stars and a wish' feedback.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which lens was hardest to judge, and why?
How did re-testing change your confidence in your solution?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one change you made and the evidence it helped.
Name one risk you are now sure your solution avoids.

worksheet.title: Week 9 - Core - Worksheet | Signature Solution - Refining & Finishing

questions.prompt: Maryam's team built a homework-reminder helper for their class teacher. It gave the right reminder on all 10 test cases where the team already knew the correct answer, but the teacher had to type every pupil's timetable in again each morning, so she stopped using it. Judging the solution through the three lenses, which statement is right?

options.text: It passes accuracy but fails usefulness, because it does not help the teacher do her real task.
It fails accuracy, because a solution the teacher stops using cannot be giving right answers.
It passes all three lenses, because it got every test case right.
It passes usefulness because the reminders were correct, but fails accuracy because of the extra typing.

feedback.correct: Correct - a solution can pass accuracy and still fail usefulness, because usefulness is judged against the real task the user has to do.
feedback.incorrect: Accuracy is about how often the answers are right, and usefulness is about whether the solution helps the user do their real task - here the answers were right but the task got harder.

questions.prompt: Match each lens to the test that gives you evidence for it.

right.text: Run it on ten examples where you already know the right answer, and record the score
Watch your real user do the actual task they need, using your solution
Check whether any results are unfair, and whether private data could be seen

feedback.correct: Correct - each lens has its own test, so a judgement only counts when it comes from the matching kind of evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Check the criteria card: accuracy is tested with known answers, usefulness against the user's real task, and risk by looking for unfair results and exposed private data.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order the lesson says to refine a solution and prove the change helped.

items.text: Judge the solution against accuracy, usefulness and risk
Choose the one improvement that matters most to your user
Make that change to the solution
Re-test the same known-answer cases and compare with the earlier score
Write the refinement note saying what changed and what the evidence shows

feedback.correct: Correct - you judge first so the change is chosen for a reason, and you re-test afterwards so you have evidence rather than a feeling.
feedback.incorrect: The order matters: judge against the lenses, choose the one improvement your user needs most, make it, re-test the same cases, then record the evidence.

questions.prompt: Omar re-runs his ten known-answer cases after making a change, and his score rises from 6 out of 10 to 9 out of 10. He writes in his refinement note that the change worked. He compared only the two totals and never looked at which cases changed, so he does not know whether a case that used to pass now fails. Is that enough evidence?

feedback.correct: Correct - the lesson asks for accuracy up AND nothing else broken. Two totals cannot show that: 6 to 9 is the same arithmetic whether three cases improved, or four improved while one that used to pass now fails.
feedback.incorrect: A higher total is not proof on its own. 6 to 9 looks the same whether three cases improved or four improved and one broke, so you have to compare case by case.

questions.prompt: A team says their change made the solution better. Which of these count as evidence for that claim, rather than opinion? Choose all that apply.

options.text: The score on the same ten known-answer tests went from 6 out of 10 to 9 out of 10
Their partner said the new version looks much nicer
Re-running the cases that already worked showed that all of them still pass
The team felt more confident once the change was made
Their real user finished the task the solution was designed for, which they could not do before

feedback.correct: Correct - evidence comes from testing that someone else could repeat, not from how the team feels about the change.
feedback.incorrect: Evidence has to come from testing: scores on known-answer cases, re-running the cases that already passed, or the real user managing the task. How something looks or feels is an opinion.

formative.targets: Self- and peer-evaluation against the tiered rubric (Emerging = expected)
formative.check: Structured self/peer review using the rubric; one improvement acted upon
formative.successCriteria: Meets the Emerging criteria; names an accuracy/usefulness/risk judgement and one improvement.
